reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome dominated by mood symptoms that markedly impair function and relationships
The defining feature is the timing: symptoms appear in the luteal phase, remit shortly after menstruation begins, and are absent in the follicular phase
Core symptoms include marked irritability, mood lability, depressed mood, anxiety, and a sense of being overwhelmed, alongside physical complaints such as bloating and breast tenderness
Diagnosis should be confirmed by prospective daily symptom charting across at least two cycles rather than by retrospective recall alone
It must be distinguished from premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying mood or anxiety disorder, which persists throughout the cycle
Serotonergic antidepressants are a first-line treatment and can be given continuously or restricted to the luteal phase according to principle
Suppressing ovulation, for example with combined hormonal contraception, can relieve symptoms by abolishing the cyclical hormonal trigger
Lifestyle measures, cognitive behavioural therapy, and attention to suicide risk during the luteal phase are important adjuncts
reference.pathophysiology: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is thought to arise from an abnormal central nervous system sensitivity to the normal cyclical fluctuations of ovarian steroids rather than from any abnormal hormone level. Progesterone metabolites such as allopregnanolone, which modulate GABA-A receptor function, and interactions with serotonergic neurotransmission appear central, so susceptible women experience marked mood and behavioural symptoms during the luteal phase when these hormones fluctuate. Because the trigger is ovulatory cycling, symptoms resolve when the cycle ends and can be abolished by suppressing ovulation. The rapid response to serotonergic agents, often faster than in major depression, supports a serotonergic mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Premenstrual exacerbation of major depressive or anxiety disorder
additionalInvestigations: Prospective daily symptom diary over at least two menstrual cycles to confirm cyclical timing
Mental health assessment to exclude an underlying mood or anxiety disorder
Thyroid function testing where clinically indicated
Screening for depression severity and suicide risk
Review of contraceptive and other medication effects on mood
redFlags: Suicidal ideation, which may intensify during the luteal phase
Symptoms persisting throughout the cycle, suggesting a primary psychiatric disorder rather than PMDD
Severe functional impairment or inability to maintain work and relationships
Features suggesting bipolar disorder that would alter treatment choice
reference.prognosis: With accurate diagnosis and treatment, most women achieve substantial symptom control; symptoms recur if treatment stops while ovulatory cycles continue and typically resolve after the menopause or with sustained ovulation suppression.
pitfalls: Diagnosing on retrospective history without prospective symptom charting
Missing an underlying mood disorder that is merely worsened premenstrually
Attributing all cyclical physical symptoms to PMDD without considering other causes
